name: Matanawí
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Valio Antunes Alves, Diego. 2019. Langue matanawí: Description phonologique et proposition de classification linguistique. Mémoire de Master 2 (Langue et Informatique), Sorbonne Université (dir. C. Montacié, H. Gérardin), 86 pp. doi:10.13140/RG.2.2.31275.71208.
catalog_locator: §5.1.1 'Considérations générales sur la prosodie', pp. 43-44; also §4.1.1 retranscription table p. 25 (acute = 'voyelle tonique', intensity accent, not tone); §5.1.3 pp. 58-59 (no secondary accents transcribed); Annexe 2 p. 83 (Nimuendajú's key 'á tontragender Vokal = Voyelle tonique').
catalog_quote: Par rapport à la tonicité, l'accent tonique primaire est indiqué dans 326 des 415 mots du matanawí. De manière générale, cet accent se porte sur la dernière syllabe du mot. ... Pour les mots polysyllabiques, l'allongement correspond à la voyelle tonique. Compte-tenu de ces observations, il semble bien possible que la longueur des voyelles et l'accent tonique n'aient pas de valeur phonologique dans la langue matanawí.
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

new_statements.quote: p. 43: « Par rapport à la tonicité, l’accent tonique primaire est indiqué dans 326 des 415 mots du matanawí. De manière générale, cet accent se porte sur la dernière syllabe du mot. » p. 44: « Compte-tenu de ces observations, il semble bien possible que la longueur des voyelles et l’accent tonique n’aient pas de valeur phonologique dans la langue matanawí. » p. 25: « Nimuendajú ne décrit pas la langue matanawí comme une langue à tons, ainsi, il semble que comme dans la langue maxali, il s’agit d’un accent primaire (augmentation de l’intensité). »
new_statements.translation: p. 43: 'As regards stress, primary stress is marked in 326 of the 415 Matanawí words. In general, this stress falls on the last syllable of the word.' p. 44: 'Given these observations, it seems quite possible that vowel length and stress have no phonological value in Matanawí.' p. 25: 'Nimuendajú does not describe Matanawí as a tone language, so it seems that, as in Maxakalí, this is a primary (intensity) stress.'
new_statements.citation: Valio Antunes Alves, Diego. 2019. Langue matanawí: Description phonologique et proposition de classification linguistique. MA thesis, Université de la Sorbonne, 86 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: The language is not in the catalog and had no existing stress statement; earlier passes found only word-by-word stress marks in Nimuendajú 1925/1922 with no prose rule. Alves 2019 supplies the first explicit generalisation (final-syllable primary stress, probably non-contrastive, non-tonal), derived from those same marks — it adds a rule where the record was silent rather than confirming or contradicting a prior placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (as marked by Nimuendajú's acute 'tontragender Vokal' diacritic on 326 of 415 lexical entries) generally falls on the word-final syllable; the author finds only 3 of 23 doublet pairs differing in stress/length with no meaning difference and concludes stress (and vowel length) are probably not contrastive; the language is explicitly treated as non-tonal (stress = intensity accent). All of this is a re-analysis of Nimuendajú 1925, not new field data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None available: the author states twice (pp. 58-59) that Nimuendajú transcribed no secondary accents, so syllabification of glide sequences such as [awij'ã] cannot be checked.
new_statements.exceptions: 'De manière générale' signals that final stress is a tendency, not exceptionless; non-final marks occur in the list (e.g. the doublets ['ai] ~ [a'i] 'plant sp.', [ʧiw'ɨ] ~ [ʧiwɨ] 'old', cited p. 44 as free variation); stress is unmarked on 89 of 415 entries; in polysyllables marked vowel length coincides with the stressed vowel (p. 44); lengthening in monosyllables attributed to citation-form pronunciation.
new_statements.identity_note: All Matanawí data come from a single speaker (João Comprido) recorded by Nimuendajú at Surupy, lower Rio Marmelos, in 1922; Alves 2019 re-transcribes that list into IPA and adds no new variety or speaker.

sources.note: The only phonological description of the language (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a phonology; comparative'); built on Nimuendajú 1925, it is the one place a stated stress/accent generalisation for Matanawí could exist. Would supersede the wordlist-only situation.
No rule; gives an IPA re-transcription of Nimuendajú's forms with stress marks (e.g. [matanawˈɨ], kajaˈri, anawˈa, huˈra, tipiˈti, muˈra), mostly final, citing Alves 2019 and Loukotka 1968.

sources.note: Nothing on Matanawí stress; the only 'stress placement' passage (p. 4) is about Pirahã syllable weight. States that Nimuendajú 1925 'remains, to this day, the entire corpus available for the language' (p. 8) and that Alves 2019 relied exclusively on Nimuendajú 1925 (p. 10), citing Alves 2019 pp. 41-42, 71, 75, 84.

sources.citation: Nimuendajú, Curt. 1925. As tribus do Alto Madeira. Journal de la Société des Américanistes 17: 137-172. Section 'V. Vocabulario Matanawí' pp. 166-171 (wordlist + short phrases from one speaker, João Comprido, Surupy, lower Marmelos, Jan./Nov. 1922); transcription key p. 148 fn. 1.
sources.note: No prose statement. The only remark is the transcription key (p. 148 fn. 1, 'Diakritische Zeiche'): 'á tontragender Vokal' (acute = tone/stress-bearing vowel), repeated on pp. 166-168 as 'o̜, tontragender Vokal'. Stress is marked word by word in the Matanawí list; in the marked forms the acute falls predominantly on the last syllable (e.g. wisá 'terra', ayá 'pedra', apí 'agua', kayarí 'Rio Madeira', anawá 'canoa', hurá 'remo', tipití, matanawí, murá), with a few non-final marks (e.g. yátamuá 'pagé'). That distributional observation is mine, not the source's; the entire Matanawí corpus is this…
